title: Asset size threshold and regulatory burden on bank profitability

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)  

Why: The regulatory burden switches on mechanically once a bank’s assets exceed $10 billion. Hence “treatment” (extra regulation) is determined entirely by whether the running variable (log assets, normalised) crosses a known cutoff (0.5). A sharp RDD exploits this deterministic rule and compares outcomes for banks infinitesimally above vs. below the cutoff.

Key assumptions  
1. Continuity: In the absence of treatment, the expected ROA would evolve smoothly through the cutoff.  
2. No precise manipulation: Banks cannot perfectly sort on either side of the $10 b threshold. We will probe this with a McCrary density test.  
3. Local comparability: Within an optimally chosen bandwidth, banks just above/below the cutoff are similar on unobservables.

## 2. R Code
```r
############################################################
#  Regulatory burden and bank profitability – Sharp RDD
############################################################

# 1. Packages ------------------------------------------------
required <- c("tidyverse", "rdrobust", "rddensity")
invisible(lapply(required, function(p) {
  if (!require(p, character.only = TRUE)) install.packages(p, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  library(p, character.only = TRUE)
}))

# 2. Load data ----------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s28_data.csv",
               col_types = cols(
                 running_var  = col_double(),
                 treated      = col_integer(),
                 y            = col_double(),
                 near_cutoff  = col_integer()
               ))

# 3. Settings -----------------------------------------------
cutoff <- 0.5       # regulatory threshold in normalised units

# 4. Core RDD estimate --------------------------------------
r_main <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$running_var, c = cutoff)
cat("\n=== Main RD (bias-corrected, local linear) ===\n")
print(summary(r_main))

# Extract and display the point estimate (bias-corrected)
tau_hat  <- r_main$Estimate[1, "tau_BC"]
se_tau   <- r_main$Estimate[1, "se_tau_BC"]
p_value  <- r_main$Estimate[1, "p_tau_BC"]

cat(sprintf("\nTreatment effect at cutoff (ROA change): %.4f  (SE = %.4f, p = %.3f)\n",
            tau_hat, se_tau, p_value))

# 5. McCrary density test -----------------------------------
cat("\n=== McCrary density test (manipulation check) ===\n")
dens_test <- rddensity(X = df$running_var, c = cutoff)
print(summary(dens_test))

# 6. Robustness checks --------------------------------------

# 6a. Different bandwidths
bandwidths <- c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30)
cat("\n=== RD estimates with ad-hoc bandwidth choices ===\n")
rbw_out <- map_df(bandwidths, function(h){
  tmp <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = cutoff, h = h)
  tibble(h = h,
         tau = tmp$Estimate[1, "tau_BC"],
         se  = tmp$Estimate[1, "se_tau_BC"],
         p   = tmp$Estimate[1, "p_tau_BC"])
})
print(rbw_out)

# 6b. Higher-order polynomial
r_poly2 <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = cutoff, p = 2)
cat("\n=== RD with quadratic control (p = 2) ===\n")
print(summary(r_poly2))

# 6c. Symmetric sample very close to cutoff (|running_var - c| < 0.1)
df_narrow <- df %>% filter(abs(running_var - cutoff) < 0.1)
r_narrow  <- rdrobust(df_narrow$y, df_narrow$running_var, c = cutoff)
cat("\n=== Very local estimate (±0.1 window) ===\n")
print(summary(r_narrow))
```

The script:
• Reads the dataset  
• Computes the bias-corrected local–linear RD estimate with `rdrobust`  
• Reports the coefficient, standard error and p-value  
• Performs the McCrary density test for manipulation  
• Re-estimates using alternative bandwidths, a quadratic specification, and a very narrow window

## 3. Expected Findings  
Economic intuition suggests the additional compliance costs that kick in at $10 billion depress profitability. I therefore expect:  
• Sign: Negative.  
• Magnitude: Roughly ‑0.002 to ‑0.004 in ROA (-20 – 40 basis points), i.e. a modest but economically meaningful decline.  
If the assumptions hold, the main RD estimate should be negative and statistically significant; robustness checks should yield similar (perhaps slightly attenuated) effects, and the McCrary test should show no significant discontinuity in the density of log assets at the cutoff.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Sharp RDD — asset threshold; test for bunching below $10B; local linear regression
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Banks just above threshold have lower ROA than just-below peers
